entries.name: Petworth
entries.honors: Petworth, a town in West Sussex, England
entries.summary: Colonel John Tayloe bought roughly 200 acres north of Rock Creek Church Road in 1803 and called his estate Petworth after the English town. Developers bought it from Tayloe heirs in 1887, merged it with the Marshall Brown estate, and filed a 387-acre subdivision plat in 1889.

sources.title: Behind the Name: Petworth (DCist, 2011)

entries.name: Grant Circle NW
entries.honors: Ulysses S. Grant, Union general and U.S. president
entries.summary: The circle at New Hampshire and Illinois Avenues honors Ulysses S. Grant. Wikipedia, citing 1889 Evening Star and Washington Post reports, says it first appeared on the Petworth plan as Sheridan Circle and was renamed in 1889. With Sherman Circle it echoes the scale of L'Enfant's circles.

entries.name: Sherman Circle NW
entries.honors: William Tecumseh Sherman, Union Civil War general
entries.summary: This circle where Illinois and Kansas Avenues meet 7th and Crittenden Streets honors General William Tecumseh Sherman. It appears on the original 1889 Petworth plat, though the circle and its four small triangle parks were not formally created until 1923.

sources.title: Sherman Circle - Wikipedia (cites NPS Cultural Landscapes 'Sherman Circle' entry)

entries.name: Georgia Avenue NW
entries.summary: Built as the Seventh Street road and later called Brightwood Avenue. Georgia Senator Augustus Bacon, unhappy with the run-down street then called Georgia Avenue in Southeast, pushed to move his state's name here. After failed tries in 1906 and 1907, an appropriations bill swapped them; old Georgia Avenue became Potomac.
entries.named: 1908 (appropriations bill; Ghosts of DC calls it the 1909 bill)

sources.title: Georgia Avenue: The Politics Behind the Name Change (Ghosts of DC)

entries.name: New Hampshire Avenue NW
entries.summary: One of DC's state-named diagonal avenues. Its northern leg through Petworth came from a 1907-08 push to extend it toward Maryland, with a bill co-sponsored by New Hampshire Senator Jacob Gallinger; a deflected route to the state line was approved around 1912-13.

sources.title: New Hampshire Avenue - Wikipedia (cites Washington Post articles 1907-1913)

entries.name: Kansas Avenue NW
entries.summary: A diagonal avenue cutting through Petworth and Sherman Circle. DC's Highway Plan naming system gave broad diagonal avenues the names of states and territories, and Kansas Avenue appears on DC's roster of state-named roadways.

entries.name: Illinois Avenue NW
entries.summary: Runs from Rock Creek Church Road through both Grant and Sherman Circles toward Georgia Avenue. Like other diagonal avenues under DC's Highway Plan naming scheme, it carries a state name. An 1895 newspaper piece already treated it as laid out in Petworth.

sources.title: Highway Plan: Street Names of Washington, DC (DC Office of Planning)
List of state-named roadways in Washington, D.C. - Wikipedia

entries.name: Decatur Street NW
entries.summary: No source consulted names the person honored. In Petworth this street was earlier mapped as Xenia Street, per turn-of-century fire insurance maps; it took its current name in the citywide renaming that fitted subdivisions to the alphabetical system.

entries.name: Buchanan Street NW
entries.summary: Namesake not documented in sources consulted. Ghosts of DC says Petworth's Buchanan Street was earlier mapped as Vallejo Street before the early-1900s renaming; a Crestwood list quoted by DCist pairs Buchanan with Zanesville instead, likely reflecting a different subdivision's old names.

sources.title: Petworth: From Rural to Hipsters (Ghosts of DC)

entries.name: Varnum Street NW
entries.summary: Namesake not documented in sources consulted. Ghosts of DC, using early Sanborn maps, says Petworth's Varnum Street was formerly Savannah Street; an 1895 newspaper sketch of Petworth already mentions Savannah Street as laid out.

sources.title: Petworth: From Rural to Hipsters (Ghosts of DC)

entries.name: Allison Street NW
entries.summary: Namesake not documented in sources consulted. Wikipedia, citing a Washington Post 'New Street Names' article of August 2, 1905, says Petworth's Utica Street became Allison Street. Allison opens the three-syllable third alphabet that follows Webster.

sources.title: Petworth (Washington, D.C.) - Wikipedia (cites Washington Post, Aug. 2, 1905)

entries.name: Tenleytown
entries.summary: The village grew around John Tennally's tavern at the fork of River Road and the Rockville road, shown on a 1791 survey. Tennally signed with an X, so spellings varied; a post office opened as Tennallytown in 1846, and 'Tenleytown' won out in the 20th century.

entries.name: Tenley Circle
entries.summary: A 1902 park plan proposed a circle where Wisconsin and Nebraska Avenues meet. The District Commissioners gave it the Tenley name in May 1927. Unusually, Wisconsin Avenue runs straight through its center. Metro's planned 'Tenley Circle' station opened as Tenleytown after residents objected.

sources.title: Tenley Circle - Wikipedia (cites Evening Star, May 28, 1927, 'Circle Named Tenley')
Behind the Name: Tenleytown (DCist, 2012)

entries.name: Wisconsin Avenue NW
entries.summary: Georgetown's stretch was High Street; north of town it was the Tennallytown or Georgetown-Rockville road. Commissioners recommended the Wisconsin name in 1890, Georgetown's portion changed in 1895, and after local protest in 1904 the name was carried through Tenleytown to the Maryland line about 1905-06.

sources.title: Wisconsin Avenue: From High Street to a State Name (Ghosts of DC)

entries.name: Nebraska Avenue NW
entries.summary: A state-named diagonal that meets Wisconsin Avenue at Tenley Circle, following the Highway Plan practice of naming broad diagonals for states. It was called Chain Bridge Road until 1906.

sources.title: Highway Plan: Street Names of Washington, DC (DC Office of Planning)
List of state-named roadways in Washington, D.C. - Wikipedia

entries.name: River Road NW
entries.summary: One of Tenleytown's founding roads: a 1791 survey of River Road shows Tennally's Tavern where it met the road now called Wisconsin Avenue, and the village grew around that junction. No source consulted explains the road's name.

sources.title: Tenleytown Historical Society (home page history)

entries.name: Fort Reno Park
entries.honors: Maj. Gen. Jesse Lee Reno, Union officer
entries.summary: Begun in 1861 by Pennsylvania troops as Fort Pennsylvania, the earthwork was renamed in 1863 for General Jesse Lee Reno, mortally wounded at South Mountain in September 1862. The fort was later demolished for an underground reservoir, and the grounds are now a park.

sources.title: Fort Reno (National Park Service)
Fort Reno Park - Wikipedia (cites Cooling & Owen, Mr. Lincoln's Forts)

entries.name: Reno (Reno City)
entries.honors: Named after Fort Reno, beside which it grew
entries.summary: A largely Black community that formed around Fort Reno during the Civil War and was subdivided in 1869; developers marketed it as Reno City. In the 1920s the city bought out and condemned its properties for the park and schools. The 1903 Jesse Reno School survives.

sources.title: Reno City (DC Historic Sites, DC Preservation League)
Fort Reno Park - Wikipedia

entries.name: Friendship Heights
entries.honors: The colonial land grant called Friendship
entries.summary: Takes its name from Friendship, a grant of about 3,000 acres given to Thomas Addison and James Stoddert in 1713. Addison descendant John Murdock later built a house called Friendship on the tract. Developers subdivided the Wisconsin Avenue area around 1900.

sources.title: Murdock's Friendship (Tenleytown Historical Society)
Ten Facts You May Not Know About Friendship Heights (DCist, 2019)

entries.name: Grant Road NW
entries.summary: A pre-grid country lane from Tenleytown eastward, first called New Cut Road and labeled Grant Road by 1870. Residents commonly assume it honors Ulysses S. Grant, who inspected the city's defenses in 1864, but the local history article treats that as unproven. Short historic blocks survive near Albemarle Street.

sources.title: Grant Road: The historic country lane in DC's modern street grid (Forest Hills Connection, 2017)

entries.name: Glover Park
entries.honors: Charles Carroll Glover, president of Riggs Bank
entries.summary: Banker Charles C. Glover bought most of butcher Henry Kengla's estate at auction in 1907 and added more Kengla land in 1911. In 1924 he gave the Foundry Branch valley for a park. Two years later developer Benjamin Gruver began advertising a new subdivision, and the name Glover Park first appeared in print.

sources.title: A Brief History of Glover Park (Glover Park History, Carlton Fletcher)
Glover Park - Wikipedia

entries.name: Tunlaw Road NW
entries.honors: Tunlaw Farm (the name is 'walnut' spelled backward)
entries.summary: Named for Tunlaw Farm, now Wesley Heights; an 1868 newspaper credits Thomas L. Hume with christening it. A resident's memoir says the farm's walnut trees inspired the reversed spelling. In 1879 a freeholders' jury condemned land for a Tunlaw Street from Back Street to High Street as an outlet for the new road, whose lower stretch followed Back Street.

sources.title: The Origins of Tunlaw Road (Glover Park History)

entries.name: Huidekoper Place NW
entries.honors: Frederic Wolters Huidekoper, Pennsylvania railroad investor and developer
entries.summary: Glover Park History files this street under Frederic W. Huidekoper, who between 1886 and 1908 laid groundwork for Burleith and southern Glover Park. The short stretch south of W Street is what remains of his Northwest Highlands subdivision, mostly condemned later for Whitehaven Park. Until 1871 Georgetown's northern boundary ran just west of it.

sources.title: Street Names of Glover Park (Glover Park History, Carlton Fletcher)
A Brief History of Glover Park (Glover Park History, Carlton Fletcher)

entries.name: Hall Place NW
entries.honors: Phillip T. Hall, first pastor of the Mount Pleasant Chapel at 35th and Wisconsin
entries.summary: Hall married the daughter of landowner Henry Weaver, and in 1903 their land became Phillip and Mary Ann Hall's Subdivision. Construction of Hall Place began in 1911; the Hall name was extended to the east-west leg between about 1912 and 1916. A resident interviewed in 1988 said it was named for Mr. Hall, who lived at its foot.

sources.title: Street Names of Glover Park (Glover Park History, Carlton Fletcher)

entries.name: Observatory Place NW
entries.honors: Observatory Heights, a 1909 subdivision named for the nearby Naval Observatory
entries.summary: The name first belonged to the east-west leg of today's Hall Place and moved here when Hall Place was extended. Its new location sat in Observatory Heights, a subdivision of Kengla land west of Tunlaw Road begun in 1909 that borrowed the prestige of the nearby Naval Observatory. The subdivision's name was soon forgotten.

sources.title: Street Names of Glover Park (Glover Park History, Carlton Fletcher)

entries.name: Benton Street NW
entries.honors: Probably Thomas Hart Benton, U.S. senator from Missouri (Glover Park History's best candidate)
entries.summary: Part of the two-syllable alphabet. Some of these names came from an 1872 Board of Public Works list of notable Americans meant to replace L'Enfant's lettered streets; the plan was shelved and names reused later. The board's deliberations went unrecorded, so Glover Park History calls Benton only the likeliest candidate.

sources.title: Street Names of Glover Park (Glover Park History, Carlton Fletcher)

entries.name: Beecher Street NW
entries.honors: Probably Henry Ward Beecher, Brooklyn preacher and abolitionist
entries.summary: Glover Park History's probable namesake is Henry Ward Beecher, whose Brooklyn congregation raised money in 1848 to free Mary and Emily Edmonson, two enslaved Washington sisters condemned to sale after the failed escape on the schooner Pearl, and sent them to Oberlin College.

sources.title: Street Names of Glover Park (Glover Park History, Carlton Fletcher)

entries.name: Calvert Street NW
entries.honors: The Calvert family, proprietors of colonial Maryland (which Calvert is not known)
entries.summary: Glover Park History sees no reason to doubt the Calvert family link but cannot say whether Cecil or Leonard Calvert was meant. Residents remembered this stretch as muddy Schneider's Lane, and one recalled houses being trucked away around 1929-30 shortly before Calvert Street was cut through to Tunlaw Road.

sources.title: Street Names of Glover Park (Glover Park History, Carlton Fletcher)

entries.name: Edmunds Street NW
entries.honors: Probably George Franklin Edmunds, U.S. senator from Vermont
entries.summary: Glover Park History's 'best bet' is Senator George F. Edmunds (1828-1919), a Radical Republican who voted to impeach Andrew Johnson, wrote the Edmunds Act against polygamy and helped draft the Sherman Antitrust Act.

sources.title: Street Names of Glover Park (Glover Park History, Carlton Fletcher)

entries.name: Fulton Street NW
entries.honors: Probably Robert Fulton, inventor and engineer
entries.summary: The street along Glover Park's northern edge. Glover Park History says it seems safe to assume it honors Robert Fulton, the inventor, engineer and artist, though no naming record is cited.

sources.title: Street Names of Glover Park (Glover Park History, Carlton Fletcher)

entries.name: Whitehaven Parkway NW
entries.honors: Whitehaven, a colonial land tract named for the English port
entries.summary: Began as West Street in the 1770 addition to Georgetown and became Madison Street in 1818, then went by Y, V and U Street between 1895 and 1925. The District bought land in 1925 for a parkway toward the Whitehaven tract in today's Palisades. After the Three Sisters Bridge died in the early 1970s, the right-of-way became Whitehaven Park.

sources.title: Street Names of Glover Park (Glover Park History, Carlton Fletcher)
Old Streets of Upper Georgetown (Glover Park History, Carlton Fletcher)

entries.name: Manor Place NW
entries.summary: The District decided in 1906 to open 'Minor street' here; a 1911 map shows Manor Street, though assessments still said Minor Street in 1917-18. It became Manor Place in the 1940s, duplicating an older Manor Place near Howard University. Glover Park History notes there never was a manor.

sources.title: Street Names of Glover Park (Glover Park History, Carlton Fletcher)

entries.name: Glover-Archbold Park
entries.honors: Charles Carroll Glover and Anne Archbold, who donated the land
entries.summary: In 1924 Glover gave 77 acres in the Foundry Branch valley; Anne Archbold added 28 at the south end. A 100-foot parkway right-of-way, marked Arizona Avenue, nearly became a four-lane highway after World War II. Archbold and C. Carroll Glover Jr. sued in 1961, and the District finally gave up the corridor in 1967.

sources.title: Glover-Archbold Parkway (Glover Park History)
Glover Park - Wikipedia

entries.name: Georgetown
entries.honors: Uncertain: King George II, or founders George Gordon and George Beall
entries.summary: In 1751 Maryland's legislature authorized buying 60 acres from George Gordon and George Beall for a town, surveyed in 1752. It was founded under King George II, and some think it was named for him; another theory credits the two Georges. Georgetown governed itself until 1871, and an 1895 act renamed its streets.

sources.title: Georgetown (Washington, D.C.) - Wikipedia

entries.name: M Street NW
entries.summary: East of Wisconsin Avenue this was Bridge Street, and west of it Falls Street, until the 1895 act made Georgetown's names match Washington's lettered grid. An 1814 map shows a bridge over Rock Creek at its end, but Georgetown Metropolitan notes the name was in use long before, so it may have been aspirational.

sources.title: Georgetown street renaming - Wikipedia
M Street (Washington, D.C.) - Wikipedia
Where the Streets Had Old Names (Georgetown Metropolitan, 2020)

entries.name: Wisconsin Avenue NW
entries.summary: Georgetown's main street was High Street, documented by 1755, the English term for a town's commercial spine; below M Street it was Water Street. North of town it was Tennallytown Road. The commissioners chose Wisconsin in 1890, and the 1895 act imposed it in Georgetown, though maps showed High Street until 1899.

sources.title: Wisconsin Avenue: From High Street to a State Name (Ghosts of DC)
Georgetown street renaming - Wikipedia
Where the Streets Had Old Names (Georgetown Metropolitan, 2020)

entries.name: Water Street NW / K Street NW
entries.summary: The 1895 renaming turned Water Street into K Street, but west of 33rd Street the Postal Service still accepts both. Greater Greater Washington's search for the District's oldest street name settled tentatively on Water Street, while noting that in 1751 this waterfront was called The Keys and West Landing.

sources.title: Georgetown street renaming - Wikipedia
What's the oldest continuously named street in DC? (Greater Greater Washington)

entries.name: Dumbarton Street NW
entries.honors: The Rock of Dumbarton, Ninian Beall's 1703 land grant, named for the rock at Dumbarton, Scotland
entries.summary: Scotsman Ninian Beall named his 1703 tract after the great rock at Dumbarton, a name that also survives in Dumbarton House and Dumbarton Oaks. Maps into the 1870s spell the street Dunbarton. It kept its name, with the spelling adjusted, in 1895, and some addresses still say Dumbarton Avenue.

entries.name: Prospect Street NW
entries.summary: One of the few old Georgetown names to survive the 1895 renaming, along with Olive Street to the east and Dumbarton, because these streets did not line up with Washington's lettered grid.

sources.title: Georgetown street renaming - Wikipedia

entries.name: Thomas Jefferson Street NW
entries.summary: Known simply as Jefferson Street until the 1895 renaming. Georgetown Metropolitan's editor has written that he doubts the original name honored Thomas Jefferson; no source consulted settles who it was for.

sources.title: Georgetown street renaming - Wikipedia
Where the Streets Had Old Names (Georgetown Metropolitan, 2020)

entries.name: 33rd Street NW
entries.summary: Market Street before 1895. A 1755 map of Beatty and Hawkins' Addition already uses the name and shows a planned market house between today's O and P Streets, decades before Georgetown's first municipal market opened on M Street in 1795. South of M it was Duck Lane in 1751, and north of M, West Lane.

sources.title: Georgetown street renaming - Wikipedia

entries.name: 31st Street NW
entries.summary: Congress Street before the 1895 renaming. On the 1751 town plan the stretch south of M Street was Fishing Lane and the part north of it East Lane, names Georgetown Metropolitan says were probably closer to alleys than streets.

sources.title: Georgetown street renaming - Wikipedia
Where the Streets Had Old Names (Georgetown Metropolitan, 2020)

entries.name: Volta Place NW
entries.summary: West of Wisconsin Avenue this was Fourth Street until the 1895 renaming; the short street had no counterpart east of Wisconsin. No source consulted explains the choice of the Volta name.

sources.title: Georgetown street renaming - Wikipedia

entries.name: Reservoir Road NW
entries.summary: West of Wisconsin Avenue, Georgetown's Seventh Street became Reservoir Road in the 1895 renaming, while Sixth Street became Dent Place and Fifth Street became Q Street.

sources.title: Georgetown street renaming - Wikipedia

entries.name: Whitehurst Freeway
entries.honors: Herbert C. Whitehurst, director of the D.C. highway department
entries.summary: The elevated road over K and Water Streets was under construction when Whitehurst died in September 1948. His successor proposed naming it for him, citing bridges and underpasses he built, and the commissioners agreed. It opened on October 8, 1949; Whitehurst's granddaughter cut the ribbon.

sources.title: U.S. Route 29 in the District of Columbia / Whitehurst Freeway - Wikipedia (cites Evening Star, Sept. 9, 1948)

entries.name: Adams Morgan
entries.honors: The John Quincy Adams and Thomas P. Morgan elementary schools
entries.summary: In May 1955 Florence Cornell, principal of the white Adams School, and Bernice Brown, principal of the Black Morgan School, started the Adams-Morgan Better Neighborhood Conference. The group's name outlived it and stuck to an area earlier sold as subdivisions such as Washington Heights and Lanier Heights.

entries.name: Old Morgan School Place NW
entries.summary: Dedicated in 2006 on what had been the block of Champlain Street just south of Marie Reed School. The Morgan School stood at California and Champlain Streets until it was demolished around 1971. Thomas P. Morgan had been D.C. police chief in 1878-79 and a District commissioner from 1879 to 1883.

sources.title: Putting the Morgan Back in Adams Morgan (DCist, 2006)
Adams Morgan: Two Schools Behind the Neighborhood's Name (Ghosts of DC)

entries.name: Columbia Road NW
entries.honors: Columbian College, today's George Washington University
entries.summary: Adams Morgan's main east-west street, forking from Connecticut Avenue and running past 16th Street to the McMillan Reservoir. Wikipedia says it was named for Columbian College rather than the District. An electric streetcar line opened on it in 1897, spurring building in Lanier Heights.

entries.name: Lanier Place NW
entries.summary: Runs through Lanier Heights, the subdivision Elizabeth Lanier Dunn and her husband, retired Gen. William M. Dunn, laid out in 1883. Its loose street pattern predates the 1888 law requiring new streets to follow the city grid. No source consulted states who the street itself is named for.

sources.title: Lanier Heights - Wikipedia

entries.name: Kalorama Road NW
entries.summary: Shares its name with Kalorama, Greek for 'nice view,' the name given in 1807 to the old Widow's Mite tract that took in today's Kalorama Triangle and Sheridan-Kalorama. No source consulted records when the road got the name.

sources.title: Kalorama Triangle Historic District - Wikipedia

entries.name: California Street NW
entries.summary: One of only two state-named roadways in the District that are not avenues. The main segment was T Street until 1901, and a short segment near Florida Avenue was V Street until 1911.

sources.title: List of state-named roadways in Washington, D.C. - Wikipedia

entries.name: Florida Avenue NW
entries.summary: Originally Boundary Street, the northern edge of L'Enfant's planned city. After Washington grew past the old limits, it was renamed in 1890.

sources.title: List of state-named roadways in Washington, D.C. - Wikipedia
Florida Avenue - Wikipedia

entries.name: Wyoming Avenue NW
entries.summary: A residential state-named avenue in Kalorama running from Kalorama Road to 18th Street.

sources.title: List of state-named roadways in Washington, D.C. - Wikipedia

entries.name: Duke Ellington Bridge
entries.honors: Duke Ellington, jazz pianist and composer
entries.summary: Carries Calvert Street over Rock Creek from 18th Street to Connecticut Avenue. It replaced a Rock Creek Railway iron truss bridge finished in 1891 and opened in 1935 as the Calvert Street Bridge, designed by Paul Cret. No source consulted gives the date of the Ellington name.

sources.title: Duke Ellington Bridge - Wikipedia

entries.name: Meridian Hill Park
entries.honors: A meridian marker placed on the hill in 1804
entries.summary: Commodore David Porter bought the land, then called Peter's Hill, in 1816 and renamed it Meridian Hill after an 1804 marker for a national meridian. The park straddles the Adams Morgan-Columbia Heights line along 16th Street. Activists later renamed it Malcolm X Park, a name still widely used.

sources.title: Meridian Hill Park - Wikipedia

entries.name: Dupont Circle
entries.honors: Rear Adm. Samuel Francis Du Pont, Union naval officer
entries.summary: The Army Corps of Engineers began the circle in 1871 as Pacific Circle, following L'Enfant's plan. Congress renamed it on February 25, 1882, and a statue of Du Pont was unveiled in 1884. The family moved the statue to Wilmington in 1917 and commissioned the present fountain by Daniel Chester French.

sources.title: Dupont Circle - Wikipedia

entries.name: Swann Street NW
entries.honors: Believed to be Thomas Swann, Maryland governor and congressman; rededicated to William Dorsey Swann
entries.summary: The street is believed to have been named for Thomas Swann, a 19th-century Maryland governor and congressman. In 2022 the Dupont Circle ANC passed a resolution dedicating it instead to William Dorsey Swann, a formerly enslaved Washingtonian known as the first person to call himself a queen of drag. A marker went up in 2025 at T Street Park.

sources.title: Swann Street Has a New Name: Swann Street (Washingtonian, 2022)
William Dorsey Swann - Wikipedia

entries.name: Massachusetts Avenue NW
entries.summary: Part of L'Enfant's 1791 plan and, at 160 feet, tied with Pennsylvania Avenue as the widest road in the city. The two run in parallel and were named for the two states that led in securing independence. Mansions rose along it near the circle in the 1870s and 1880s, and it is now Embassy Row.

entries.name: Connecticut Avenue NW
entries.summary: L'Enfant drew it in 1791 from the White House to Boundary Street. By the 1920s its stretch above the circle had turned commercial, with mansions replaced by shops and offices. A deck over the underpass between the circle and Q Street began construction in 2025.

sources.title: Connecticut Avenue - Wikipedia
Dupont Circle - Wikipedia

entries.name: New Hampshire Avenue NW
entries.summary: A state-named diagonal through the circle. Its southern section runs from F Street near the Kennedy Center to 15th Street and Florida Avenue; a separate northern section runs from Columbia Heights into Maryland.

entries.name: P Street NW
entries.summary: Named in 1791 when George Washington's plan gave east-west streets letters. The 1795 survey of the city's northern boundary began at the P Street ford on Rock Creek, and the first bridge there was the Paper Mill Bridge. P Street crosses the circle on its way to Georgetown.

sources.title: P Street - Wikipedia

entries.name: Florida Avenue NW
entries.summary: The historic district's northwest edge. It was Boundary Street, the northern limit of L'Enfant's city, until the city grew past it and renamed it in 1890.

sources.title: List of state-named roadways in Washington, D.C. - Wikipedia

entries.name: Rhode Island Avenue NW
entries.summary: A state-named artery that begins at M Street and Connecticut Avenue, passes Logan Circle and leaves the District in Woodridge, carrying U.S. 1 for much of its length.

sources.title: List of state-named roadways in Washington, D.C. - Wikipedia

entries.name: Cleveland Park
entries.summary: In 1886 Cleveland bought a stone farmhouse opposite Rosedale and remade it as a summer home, Oak View, nicknamed Red Top for its red roof. He sold it in 1890 to developer Francis Newlands. The Oak View and Cleveland Heights plats followed that year, then the Cleveland Park Company's subdivision of 1894. Red Top was demolished in 1927.

sources.title: Cleveland Park - Wikipedia
Cleveland Park Historic District brochure (DC Historic Preservation Office)

entries.name: Rosedale
entries.summary: Uriah Forrest, a Revolutionary War officer and congressman, built the farmhouse in 1793 around a stone cottage of about 1740, making it the oldest surviving house in Washington. His descendants held it until 1920, when Queene Coonley bought it. The grounds became a public conservancy in 2002.

sources.title: Rosedale (Washington, D.C.) - Wikipedia
Cleveland Park - Wikipedia

entries.name: Newark Street NW
entries.summary: The Cleveland Park Company's first subdivision of 1894 included Newark Street from 33rd Street to Wisconsin Avenue; Cleveland's Oak View tract had used it as its northern edge. The company built a chemical fire engine house on Newark and a streetcar waiting lodge at Connecticut Avenue, site of today's library.

sources.title: Cleveland Park Historic District brochure (DC Historic Preservation Office)

entries.name: Ordway Street NW
entries.summary: Called Omaha Street when the first Cleveland Park subdivision laid it out between 34th and 36th Streets in 1894. No source consulted says why it was renamed Ordway.

sources.title: Cleveland Park Historic District brochure (DC Historic Preservation Office)

entries.name: Reno Road NW
entries.summary: A section through Cleveland Park was once called Bridge Street, for a rustic bridge that carried it over Newark Street toward a path to the Connecticut Avenue streetcar station. The early Oak View and Cleveland Heights plats lay just west of today's Reno Road.

sources.title: Cleveland Park Historic District brochure (DC Historic Preservation Office)

entries.name: Macomb Street NW
entries.summary: Lower Macomb Street, from Ross Place up to the crest above Rock Creek, belonged to the Connecticut Avenue and Northern Additions, bought within a year of the 1894 subdivision, whose streets followed the land's contours rather than the grid. No source consulted gives the namesake.

sources.title: Cleveland Park Historic District brochure (DC Historic Preservation Office)

entries.name: Connecticut Avenue NW
entries.summary: Francis Newlands' Chevy Chase Land Company cut the avenue north from Calvert Street around 1890, bridging Rock Creek and Klingle Valley for its Rock Creek Railway. Streetcars ran by 1892, with a Cleveland Park stop soon after. The 1891 Klingle Valley trestle was replaced in 1931 by Paul Cret's Art Deco bridge.

sources.title: Cleveland Park Historic District brochure (DC Historic Preservation Office)
Connecticut Avenue - Wikipedia

entries.name: Woodley Road NW

entries.summary: One of the four state-named avenues centered on the Capitol. It survives in broken pieces, including a stretch in Southwest Waterfront between Canal and H Streets and a one-block section near the Rayburn House Office Building.

sources.title: List of state-named roadways in Washington, D.C. - Wikipedia

entries.summary: The name was a real-estate brand: the Palisades of the Potomac Land Improvement Company advertised lots here in June 1890 as a coming fashionable suburb reached by Conduit Road, electric railway and boat. Wikipedia dates the subdivision's layout to 1893; streetcars to Georgetown and Glen Echo followed two years later.

entries.summary: It began as Conduit Road, the service road above Montgomery Meigs's Washington Aqueduct conduit, which first carried Potomac water into the city in 1859. entries.honors: Gouverneur Kemble, superintendent of the West Point Foundry
entries.summary: The park keeps the earthworks of Battery Kemble, a Union gun position finished in autumn 1861 whose two 100-pounder Parrott rifles covered Chain Bridge and Virginia. It was named for Gouverneur Kemble of Cold Spring, New York, whose West Point Foundry made most of the Union's heavy guns.

entries.name: Weaver Terrace NW
entries.summary: The Palisades Community Association's history says the Weaver brothers bought farmland here in the 1850s and there were so many Weavers that three streets bore their name. One became Arizona Avenue; Weaver Terrace is the reminder that remains.

sources.title: History (Palisades Community Association)

entries.summary: One of DC's state-named avenues; it runs from Oregon Avenue past American University and becomes Loughboro Road at Chain Bridge Road. entries.summary: L'Enfant's avenue originally ended at Boundary Street. Around 1890 Congressman Francis Newlands, who had quietly bought land toward Chevy Chase, graded a straight extension with streetcar track down its center. The Bureau of Standards opened its first campus beside it at Van Ness Street in 1901, and the Taft Bridge linked both halves in 1907.

entries.summary: A country lane dating to 1859 or earlier that became a Civil War military road from Tennallytown to the forts. An 1867 map labels it New Cut Road; an 1870 map calls it Grant Road. Local historians say it is generally assumed to honor Ulysses S. Grant after his March 1864 tour of the defenses, but that is not documented.

entries.summary: A straighter Davenport Street was cut through to Forest Hills in the late 1920s.
